title: What Did Hospitality Mean in the Ancient World?
subtitle: In a world without hotels, police, or embassies, the welcome of strangers was the difference between life and death. The Bible treats it accordingly. We have made it a programming word.

sections.title: What the Road Was Like
sections.body:
Strip away everything a modern traveler takes for granted, the hotels and police and consulates, the credit cards and highway lights. A stranger arriving at a village toward evening was in real danger, and he was also dangerous, an unknown quantity with no kin nearby to vouch for him or avenge him. The ancient Near East answered this standoff with one of the oldest institutions in human history.

Hospitality turned a potential threat into a protected guest. There was water for the feet and food, the best in the house rather than the leftovers, then shelter for the night and protection under the roof, defended at the host's own cost, and after that safe passage on. The obligations bound both directions, and a community's honor rose or fell on how it treated the stranger at the edge of camp.

So when the Bible talks about welcoming strangers, it's describing a load-bearing institution of survival, one God writes himself into from Genesis onward, and not entertaining, that social grace for people with nice tables. We hear dinner party, when the text means something closer to rescue.

sections.title: Abraham Runs
sections.body:
Genesis 18 opens at the hottest hour of the day, when no one moves. Three strangers appear at the oaks of Mamre, and Abraham, an old man, runs to meet them. He bows, begs them to stay, and promises a little bread and a little water, then runs again, to the tent and to the herd, and produces a feast of fresh bread from three seahs of fine flour, a tender calf, curds and milk. That understatement was part of the form. Promise little, give everything, and stand by while they eat, a servant in your own camp.

Only as the scene unfolds does the text show its hand. Abraham has been hosting the Lord. The promise of Isaac is spoken at that meal, to a guest list he did not recognize when he ran to meet it. Hebrews 13:2 has this story in its bones. Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.

The next chapter shows the same institution inverted. The men of Sodom surround Lot's house to violate his guests. In the Bible's own categories, what Sodom does goes past violence into the murder of welcome.

sections.title: The Ger: Memory as Law
sections.body:
Israel's law has a technical word for the resident outsider, the ger, the immigrant living inside the community without land or kin to protect him. Torah returns to him with striking persistence. Do not oppress the sojourner. Leave the edges of your field and the fallen grapes for the poor and for the sojourner. One law shall apply to the native and to the ger alike. He is grouped again and again with the widow and the orphan, the three classes a society can wrong without consequence, which is exactly why God says he watches.

And the law gives its reason, and the reason is memory. You shall love the stranger as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt. Israel's ethics toward the outsider rest on Israel's own story of being the outsider. Forget the story and the welcome dies.

This is the move that should stop us. The command makes no appeal to the stranger's usefulness or his potential; it appeals to who you were when no one had to take you in, and Someone did. Every Christian doctrine of welcome starts there, with our own rescue.

sections.title: The Gospel Moved on Hospitality
sections.body:
When Jesus sends out the seventy two, the mission plan is hospitality. Take no moneybag, no knapsack, no sandals. Eat what is set before you. Stay in one house. The messengers arrive with nothing, and the kingdom enters a town through whichever door opens. Jesus himself works as a perpetual guest, at Levi's table, at Zacchaeus' house, at a Pharisee's dinner, and Luke keeps showing us that how people receive him is how they receive God. Joshua Jipp has argued that this is not a detail of the story but its shape. The gospel of a God who welcomes strangers travels by strangers being welcomed.

The early church ran on the same fuel. Romans 12:13 tells believers to pursue hospitality, and the verb is the one used for chasing something down. The word itself is philoxenia, love of the stranger. Third John turns entirely on this. Gaius is praised for supporting traveling teachers he did not know, and Diotrephes is condemned for refusing them and expelling those who would not refuse. In a church with no buildings and no budgets, the open door was the infrastructure, and missionaries, letters and the Lord's Supper itself all moved through houses.

sections.title: What the Word Demands Now
sections.body:
The church has largely turned hospitality into a programming word, meaning a committee, a coffee cart, a greeter team, a small group potluck. None of those things is wrong, but none of them is philoxenia. Having friends over is friendship, and Scripture commends it, but the biblical word means love of the stranger, the person who cannot repay you, vouch for you, or vote with you. Jesus says it without cover. When you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, because they cannot repay you.

I write this as a pastor, and I am inside the problem: most of our tables seat people we already love. The drift from stranger to friend, from rescue to entertaining, happens in our houses too, quietly, one comfortable evening at a time.

The old institution assumed something we've engineered away, that the stranger would actually reach your door. Now we have to go and find the door he's standing at. A church that recovers philoxenia won't need a better welcome program so much as open homes and a willingness to be inconvenienced by people who arrived with nothing. That was always the price of the institution, and it still is.

sources.title: Making Room: Recovering Hospitality as a Christian Tradition
